extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners and students responsible for internal/employee communications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and implementing internal communications (vision/mission, policies, media, listening and connection strategies) to socialize, inform, and engage employees and other internal publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vision statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The vision statement represents a future goal that outlines general priorities for where the organization is headed and answers “Why does this organization exist?” and “What would we like to accomplish?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A shared vision is integral to organizational culture and is communicated through internal relations; a well-planned vision statement helps manage reactions to changes, communicates values and strategic priorities (e.g., R&D, market share, distributor relationships). Usually created at the highest level (CEO/dominant coalition), but involving employees in creation fosters pride, ownership, responsibility and a ‘shared vision.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The mission statement answers the question: “How are we different from our competitors?” and conveys goals, organizational structure and strategy, legitimacy, values, participation and ownership among employees, leadership, responsibility to the community, ethical priorities, and commitment to publics and stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mission statements are more specific and operational than vision statements and help employees set priorities and goals so members are committed to achieving the mission; compelling mission statements emphasize strengths and provide competitive advantage by keeping members 'on strategy.' Examples include Starbucks, Peet’s, and Caribou Coffee mission statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy documents / manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy manuals specify internal policies, rights, responsibilities, bureaucratic channels, procedures, and relevant governmental laws (e.g., antitrust, insider trading), often in exhaustive book or electronic form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for reporting procedures (e.g., sexual harassment), requesting promotion, or personal use of office computers. Major drawback: sheer length and complexity make them little used; to be effective they should be well written, concise, interesting, and organized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics statements / code of ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: A code of ethics provides a guide to management’s values, priorities, standards, and policy and spells out the ethical parameters used by the organization in evaluating decision options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-written code offers more concrete guidance than a vision or mission statement but is briefer than a policy manual; also called credos, principles, beliefs, values, or standards (example: Johnson & Johnson’s credo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training materials and new-employee orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Orientation and training materials socialize new employees into organizational culture, teaching values, standards, norms, expectations, and methods of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socialization and acculturation help employees internalize organizational values; rigorous training and clear expectations build consistent decision making and allow employees to act confidently knowing the organization will stand behind them if they act according to its values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonmediated verbal communication (face-to-face)
rubrics_metrics.description: In-person verbal communication is the heart of internal communication; employees prefer direct communication from superiors and studies show it is the most memorable and effective delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings require specific objectives, careful planning and staging, and skillful direction; two-way exchange should be open but controlled to avoid diversion. For some important meetings, use trained facilitators so power, content, and process aren't vested in one person. Face-to-face is expensive but economical long-term for ideas and team-building; preferred when employee input is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grapevine monitoring and management
rubrics_metrics.description: The grapevine (word of mouth face-to-face and online) is often the quickest means for communicating information but is informal, uncontrolled, and frequently unreliable or 'enhanced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR staff should stay tuned to the grapevine and, when trouble brews, squelch gossip by releasing the full facts. The grapevine often fills information gaps left by inadequate internal communication programs and can be harmful if rumors spread about layoffs, harassment, takeovers, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meetings, teleconferences and videoconferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Meetings bring people together for two-way communication and are examples of task-oriented and larger gatherings; technology (teleconferencing, videoconferencing, podcasting) can connect distributed employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large gatherings need careful planning; technology saves travel/time/cost and enables consistent messaging, recordings allow asynchronous access (Google TGIF example). Yet face-to-face meetings remain highly valued and preferred for soliciting input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee publications and printed newsletters
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational publications (newsletters, intranet, email, newspapers, magazines, 'magapapers') are controlled media that let an organization communicate in its own words and serve as workhorses of employee communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common goals: (1) keep employees informed of strategy/goals, (2) give info needed to perform, (3) encourage standards/quality/efficiency/social responsibility, (4) recognize achievements, (5) create two-way communication for feedback. Publications can be targeted, bilingual, two-way (surveys, anonymous comments), and require top-management cooperation to respond to input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inserts and enclosures (payroll stuffers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small printed inserts placed into paycheck envelopes or direct-deposit receipts used for targeted notices or calls to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include high receptivity from a predisposed audience, strategic targeting, and economy due to light weight (low postage). Useful for legislative calls, charity recruitment, or notifying changes in benefits/procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published speeches, position papers and backgrounders
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting CEO speeches, position statements, and backgrounders on websites/intranets gives employees access to leadership ideas and organizational positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These materials help employees represent the organization externally and provide historical/contextual knowledge for new assignments. Downside: generally only information seekers will access them; organizations can reprint favorable media coverage for internal archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulletin boards and notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical or electronic bulletin boards display notices, mandated postings (OSHA, Homeland Security), brief messages, and announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulletin boards must be updated often; repeated notices become background noise and cause inattention. Typical themes: safety, health, housekeeping, productivity, and security. Use creative supplements to heighten awareness when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intranets
rubrics_metrics.description: Intranets are internal, employee-accessible systems containing email, publications, policy manuals, bulletin boards, and shared project data, allowing search and rapid information retrieval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: disseminates information widely/rapidly, empowers employees, overcomes geography, increases two-way communication and collaboration. Risks include privacy concerns (spyware/snooping software), perception of mistrust if monitored, and hacking or internal sabotage; internal publics should be involved in decisions and security threats must be communicated immediately. Consolidation/integration (IBM, Motorola examples) improves usability and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hotlines and toll-free numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Hotlines provide disseminated basic information (e.g., emergency/closing info) and can serve as anonymous whistle-blower/reporting systems for questionable practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hotlines can identify emerging trends before they become crises. Sarbanes-Oxley (section 301(4)(B)) requires anonymous reporting systems for publicly held companies; third-party centers are popular for guaranteeing anonymity and consistent documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email and e-newsletters
rubrics_metrics.description: Email is ubiquitous and a primary method for pushing information to employees; e-newsletters 'push' messages compared to intranets/websites which require employees to 'pull' information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use email for timely, targeted messages; recognize differing access to computers among employee groups (e.g., frontline staff).

rubrics_metrics.name: New media (podcasts, blogs, social media, video)
rubrics_metrics.description: New technologies (CEO podcasts, employee blogs, video, internal social networks, Facebook) are used to connect executives and employees and to extend celebrations and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools can strengthen employee relationships and attract younger talent (Millennials), but many organizations limit social media use at work due to concerns about employee statements and control of message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listening mechanisms and feedback systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should provide formal and informal channels for employees to communicate concerns and feedback (meetings, publications, hotlines, anonymous email systems, ombudsman, surveys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges: employees may fear being labeled a 'troublemaker.' Anonymous systems, hotlines, and ombuds officers can provide confidential reporting and informal mediation; surveys measure engagement and other concerns. Listening helps monitor trends and identify problems before they escalate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecting employees (social events and internal networks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal relations should connect employees to each other through company picnics, family days, and internal social networking sites (e.g., IBM’s BluePages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such connections foster collaboration, corporate culture, and can help attract and retain talent, especially younger employees; internal social networks can enable high-frequency interaction (BluePages accessed millions of times daily in example).
